x.ASV: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm of David. How long, O Jehovah? wilt thou forget me for ever? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
x.Darby: To the chief Musician. A Psalm of David. How long, Jehovah, wilt thou forget me for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
x.KJV: To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O Lord? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
x.YLT: To the Overseer. --A Psalm of David. Till when, O Jehovah, Dost Thou forget me? --for ever? Till when dost Thou hide Thy face from me?

nt: David is probably implying the words “will you forget me,” but since the next two phrases in this verse indicates what David is asking Yahweh, you do not need to fill in the implied words in this phrase.

The implication is that **forget** means “not help.” You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Will you not help me forever] or [Will you not ever answer me]

Here, **face** represents God’s attention and favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [will you continue to ignore me] or [will you keep withdrawing your favor from me]

x.ASV: How long shall I take counsel in my soul, Having sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?
x.Darby: How long shall I take counsel in my soul, with sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?
x.KJV: How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? how long shall mine enemy be exalted over me?
x.YLT: Till when do I set counsels in my soul? Sorrow in my heart daily? Till when is mine enemy exalted over me?

nt: Here, **in my soul** represents David’s whole self as he experiences emotions. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as in the UST.

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [having sorrow in my heart]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **sorrow**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [feeling sorrowful]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in my thoughts] or [in my inner being]

The implication is that David was distressed and in anguish throughout the entire daytime. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [daily] or [continually]

By **be high over me**, the psalmist means that his enemy will defeat him and triumph over him. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [will the one being hostile to me be exalted over me]

x.ASV: Consider and answer me, O Jehovah my God: Lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;
x.Darby: Consider, answer me, O Jehovah myGod! lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the [sleep of] death;
x.KJV: Consider and hear me, O Lord my God: lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;
x.YLT: Look attentively; Answer me, O Jehovah, my God, Enlighten mine eyes, lest I sleep in death,

nt: Here David is speaking of having energy and hope as if it were **light** coming into his eyes. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [restore my strength and hope] or [make me feel alive again]

David is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first asks God to help him so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the request. Alternate translation: [otherwise] or [or else]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. If it would be clearer in your language, you can supply these words from the context, as in the ULT, which supplies **sleep of**.

The psalmist is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **sleep the sleep of death**. Depending on what is helpful in your language, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [I die]

x.ASV: Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; Lest mine adversaries rejoice when I am moved.
x.Darby: Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him! [lest] mine adversaries be joyful when I am moved.
x.KJV: Lest mine enemy say, I have prevailed against him; and those that trouble me rejoice when I am moved.
x.YLT: Lest mine enemy say, `I overcame him,' Mine adversaries joy when I am moved.

nt: David is using the word translated as **Lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first asks God to help him (3) so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the request. Alternate translation: [Otherwise the one being hostile to me will say] or [Or else the one being hostile to me will say]

The psalmist is leaving out a word that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. Here the word is either “and” (which the ULT supplies) or “lest.” You can supply the word or words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [lest my adversaries rejoice]
The word the ULT translates as **when**, in this context, could mean: (1) “when” or (2) “because.” Alternate translation: [because]

The expression **I am shaken** is a passive verbal form. If your language would not use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [they shake me] or [they overcome me]

Here David is speaking of himself as if he were an object that could be **shaken**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am overcome] or [I am defeated]

x.ASV: But I have trusted in thy lovingkindness; My heart shall rejoice in thy salvation.
x.Darby: As for me, I have confided in thy loving-kindness; my heart shall be joyful in thy salvation.
x.KJV: But I have trusted in thy mercy; my heart shall rejoice in thy salvation.
x.YLT: And I, in Thy kindness I have trusted, Rejoice doth my heart in Thy salvation.

nt: The psalmist uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the possibility of his enemies triumphing over him and his trust in Yahweh’s faithfulness. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Nevertheless, I] or [However, I]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **covenant faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [in all the ways you are faithful to your covenant]
The word the ULT translates as **let my heart rejoice**, in this context, could mean: (1) “let my heart rejoice” or (2) “will rejoice.” Alternate translation: [my heart will rejoice]

Here the **heart** represents where a person’s thoughts and feelings exist. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [let everything in me rejoice]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because of the way you have saved me]

x.ASV: I will sing unto Jehovah, Because he hath dealt bountifully with me.
x.Darby: I will sing unto Jehovah, for he hath dealt bountifully with me.
x.KJV: I will sing unto the Lord, because he hath dealt bountifully with me.
x.YLT: I do sing to Jehovah, For He hath conferred benefits upon me!

nt: If it would be more natural in your language, you could reverse the order of these phrases, since the second phrase gives the reason for the result that the first phrase describes. Alternate translation: [Because Yahweh has dealt bountifully with me, I will sing to him]

David could be using the past tense **he has dealt bountifully**: (1) in order to describe something that is going to happen in the future to show that the event will certainly happen. Alternate translation: [he will deal bountifully with me] or (2) to refer to things Yahweh has done for him in the past, in which case you can translate this phrase as in the ULT.
